subQuestions.questionText: Long-term financial instruments, such as shares, are traded in the … market.
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: B - capital (2 marks)
Long-term financial instruments such as shares and bonds are traded in the capital market, whereas short-term instruments are traded in the money market.

subQuestions.questionText: Business cycles that are caused by changes in the construction industry that last for 15 to 20 years are called … cycles.
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: A - Kuznets (2 marks)
Kuznets cycles last about 15 to 20 years and are linked to changes (building/construction and infrastructure) in the construction industry.

subQuestions.questionText: Transfer of ownership of entities from the private sector to the public sector is called …
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: D - nationalisation (2 marks)
Nationalisation is the transfer of ownership of enterprises/assets from the private sector to the public sector (the state), the opposite of privatisation.

subQuestions.questionText: Investment contracts that base their value on the underlying assets, such as currencies and commodities, are known as …
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: C - financial derivatives (2 marks)
Financial derivatives are investment contracts whose value is derived from underlying assets such as currencies, commodities, shares or interest rates.

subQuestions.questionText: The international organisation that reduces tariffs and other trade barriers to liberalise trade is called the …
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: C - World Trade Organisation (2 marks)
The World Trade Organisation (WTO) promotes free trade by reducing tariffs and other trade barriers between member countries.

subQuestions.questionText: The growth and development policy that aims to eliminate poverty and reduce inequality by 2030, is known as the …
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: A - National Development Plan (2 marks)
The National Development Plan (NDP) is South Africa's long-term plan aimed at eliminating poverty and reducing inequality by 2030.

options.D: Accelerated and Shared Growth Initiative for South Africa.

subQuestions.questionText: A cash incentive that aims to provide investment in the training of the South African labour force to gain new expertise, is called the …
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: B - Skills Support Programme (2 marks)
The Skills Support Programme is a cash incentive that funds the training of the labour force so that workers gain new skills and expertise.

subQuestions.questionText: The percentage of the population living in poverty in a country is indicated by …
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: D - the headcount index (2 marks)
The headcount index measures the proportion (percentage) of the population living below the poverty line.

subQuestions.questionText:
Choose a description from COLUMN B that matches the item in COLUMN A. Write only the letter (A–I) next to the question numbers (1.2.1–1.2.8).

COLUMN A:
1.2.1 Transfer payment
1.2.2 Investment
1.2.3 Cash reserve requirements
1.2.4 Price discrimination
1.2.5 Social indicator
1.2.6 Desirable mix
1.2.7 Industrial development zones
1.2.8 Expanded Public Works Programme

COLUMN B:
A combination of international trade policies suitable for the prevailing conditions in an economy
B monitors identifiable and definable issues related to human well-being
C nationwide government intervention to create employment using labour intensive methods
D money received without any productive service rendered
E charging different customers, different prices for the same product
F spending by businesses on capital goods
G used to control money supply through buying and selling of government securities
H purpose-built industrial estates that are physically enclosed and link to international ports
I the minimum amount of money that the South African Reserve Bank requires banks to maintain in order to manipulate money creation activities
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 1 mark per correct match (8 x 1 = 8 marks):
1.2.1 Transfer payment → D (money received without any productive service rendered)
1.2.2 Investment → F (spending by businesses on capital goods)
1.2.3 Cash reserve requirements → I (the minimum amount of money that the South African Reserve Bank requires banks to maintain in order to manipulate money creation activities)
1.2.4 Price discrimination → E (charging different customers, different prices for the same product)
1.2.5 Social indicator → B (monitors identifiable and definable issues related to human well-being)
1.2.6 Desirable mix → A (combination of international trade policies suitable for the prevailing conditions in an economy)
1.2.7 Industrial development zones → H (purpose-built industrial estates that are physically enclosed and link to international ports)
1.2.8 Expanded Public Works Programme → C (a nationwide government intervention to create employment using labour intensive methods)

subQuestions.questionText: Give ONE term for the following description: When a country involved in international trade produces more output than other countries given the same input.
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: Absolute advantage (1 mark)
A country has an absolute advantage when it can produce more output than other countries using the same quantity of inputs.

subQuestions.questionText: Give ONE term for the following description: A document that details expected revenue and projected expenditure for the next fiscal year.
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: Annual budget / National budget / main budget (1 mark)
The annual (national) budget is the document that sets out government's expected revenue and projected expenditure for the coming fiscal year.

subQuestions.questionText: Give ONE term for the following description: Tax systems where low-income earners pay higher tax rates while high-income earners pay lower tax rates.
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: Regressive (1 mark)
A regressive tax takes a larger percentage of income from low-income earners than from high-income earners.

subQuestions.questionText: Give ONE term for the following description: The provision of incentives to encourage local businesses to produce goods to sell to other countries.
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: Export promotion (1 mark)
Export promotion is a trade strategy that provides incentives to encourage local businesses to produce goods for sale in foreign (export) markets.

subQuestions.questionText: Give ONE term for the following description: The process that focuses on the improvement of people's standard of living.
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: Economic development (1 mark)
Economic development is the process focused on improving people's standard of living and overall quality of life.

subQuestions.questionText: Give ONE term for the following description: The industrial development strategy that focuses on improving the competitiveness in manufacturing by considering input prices and technology.
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: Integrated Manufacturing Strategy (1 mark)
The Integrated Manufacturing Strategy aims to improve competitiveness in manufacturing by taking input prices and technology into account.

subQuestions.questionText: Name any TWO participants of the circular-flow model.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 1 mark per correct participant (2 x 1 = 2 marks). Any TWO of:
• Households
• Business sector
• Government
• Foreign sector

subQuestions.questionText: Why does public sector failure lead to social instability?
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks for a correct full-sentence response (1 x 2):
• The lives of people are destabilised, and their human rights compromised.
• The community becomes disgruntled and starts making their demands through protesting.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText:
(Refer to the table 'GROSS VALUE ADDED BY KIND OF ECONOMIC ACTIVITY' in the question paper.) Identify the base year that the South African Reserve Bank uses to compile national accounts aggregates.

GROSS VALUE ADDED BY KIND OF ECONOMIC ACTIVITY (2021 figures)
| Sector | At constant 2015 prices | At current prices |
| Primary sector | 295 203 | 472 082 |
| Secondary sector | 552 601 | 943 771 |
| Tertiary sector | 2 017 745 | 3 107 747 |
| Gross value added at basic prices | 2 865 548 | 4 523 600 |
[Adapted from SARB Quarterly Bulletin, March 2021]
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: 2015 (1 mark)
The table shows values 'at constant 2015 prices', indicating that 2015 is the base year used by the SARB.

subQuestions.questionText: Give the alternative term used for gross value added in national accounts.
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: Gross domestic product / GDP(P) (1 mark)
Gross value added at basic prices is, after adjustment, the production measure of gross domestic product (GDP by the production method).

subQuestions.questionText: Briefly describe the term gross value added.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks for a correct description:
Gross value added is the value that is added to the goods at every stage of the production process.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText: How are basic prices converted to market prices?
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks for a correct response:
Taxes on products are added to, and subsidies on products are subtracted from, gross domestic product at basic prices to arrive at gross domestic product at market prices. In other words: GVA at basic prices PLUS taxes on products MINUS subsidies on products = GDP at market prices.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText: Why would economists prefer constant prices to current prices when measuring economic growth?
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks per correct explanation (2 x 2 = 4 marks):
• Constant prices are adjusted to exclude the effects of inflation, whereas current prices are not adjusted.
• Constant prices provide a true reflection of the actual changes in the production of goods and services, while current prices give a distorted reflection.
• Current prices give a distorted indication of the actual growth of the economy.
• Measuring economic growth using constant prices provides accurate data to policy makers to make informed decisions.
• Constant prices help to make an accurate comparison of economic performance from year to year.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText:
(Refer to the extract 'PUBLIC DEBT ON THE INCREASE' in the question paper.) Name the government department responsible for the formulation and implementation of fiscal policy.

Extract: High government debt levels increase the cost of borrowing across the economy. The rising debt leads to higher future taxation and uncertainty. Servicing this rising debt takes away resources that could have been invested in infrastructure. Our borrowing requirement will remain well above R500 billion in each year of the medium term despite the modest improvements in our fiscal position. This 2021 budget framework puts South Africa on course to achieve a primary surplus. By doing this, government debt will stabilise at 88,9 per cent of gross domestic product in 2025/26. [Adapted from 2021/22 Annual Budget Statement]
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: Department of Finance (National Treasury) (1 mark)
The Department of Finance / National Treasury is responsible for the formulation and implementation of fiscal policy.

subQuestions.questionText: Give the benchmark percentage of public debt in relation to gross domestic product.
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: Not more than 60% (1 mark)
The internationally accepted benchmark for public (government) debt is not more than 60% of gross domestic product.

subQuestions.questionText: Briefly describe the term medium-term expenditure framework.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks for a correct description:
The medium-term expenditure framework shows government's income and expenditure estimates for a 3-year period.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText: Why is there a need for government to spend more on social development?
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks for a correct explanation:
• A significant number of the South African population are still living in poverty; thus the government should allocate more resources to improve their standard of living.
• The unemployment figure is among the highest in the world due to low skills levels, decreased GDP and a lack of investment. A high unemployment rate increases dependency on government, compelling it to increase spending on activities that improve people's lives.
• Many people lost their jobs and sources of income due to the Covid-19 pandemic and would need grants to survive.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText: How can income tax brackets influence taxpayers?
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks per correct explanation (2 x 2 = 4 marks):
• An increase in income can push taxpayers into higher tax brackets, if tax brackets remain the same, resulting in higher taxes (bracket creep).
• Taxpayers do not receive the full benefits of an increase in their wages.
• An increase in income will not shift households to higher tax brackets if tax brackets increase, thus preventing bracket creep.
• Tax relief will be provided to workers as their existing salary may fall in a lower tax bracket.
• Their disposable income can increase, allowing them to spend more on goods and services.
NB: Accept the explanation for a decrease in the tax bracket which will have a negative impact on the consumer's disposable income.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText: With the aid of a correctly labelled graph, explain the multiplier concept.
subQuestions.memoText:
Graph (Max 4 marks):
• Labelling of axis = 1 mark (Expenditure on vertical axis; Income on horizontal axis)
• Labelling on axis = 1 mark
• Shift of consumption/expenditure function (AE to AE1, i.e. E = C + I to E1 = C + I) = 1 mark
• 45° line showing E = Y = 1 mark

Explanation (Max 4 marks) – must relate to the graph:
• The multiplier effect occurs when a small increase in spending leads to a proportionately larger increase in national income.
• At an income of Y the expenditure curve intersects the vertical axis at AE.
• An increase from AE to AE1 means more money is injected into the economy.
• This causes a proportionately larger increase in income from Y to Y1.
(Accept any other correct relevant response. Explanation must relate to the graph in order to earn marks.)

subQuestions.questionText: How can changes in terms of trade influence the South African economy?
subQuestions.memoText:
Award up to 8 marks (2 marks per fully developed point). Maximum 2 marks for mere listing of facts/examples:
• An improvement in the terms of trade comes as a result of an increase in export prices and/or a decrease in import prices.
• An increase in export prices would increase economic welfare in the short term, as more revenue is earned with the same/less expenditure on imports.
• A decrease in import prices would result in less expenditure or fewer payments on imports in the short term.
• Higher export earnings and lower import payments may reduce the Balance of Payments deficit in the short term.
• Fewer resources would be used to produce exports to pay for imports.
• Demand for South African exports may decrease in the long run due to higher prices.
• A decrease in the terms of trade comes as a result of a decrease in export prices and/or an increase in import prices.
• A decrease in export prices would decrease economic welfare in the short term, as less revenue is earned with the same/less expenditure on imports.
• An increase in import prices would result in more expenditure or more payments on imports in the short term.
• Lower export earnings and higher import payments may increase the Balance of Payments deficit in the short term.
• More resources would be used to produce exports to pay for imports.
• Demand for South African exports may increase in the long run due to lower prices.
OR
• An increase in exports will encourage development of the country's industrial capacity.
• More foreign exchange will be earned to pay for imports.
• Increased exports may lead to an improvement of the Balance of Payments.
• An increase in imports may lead to the depreciation of the exchange rate, making it more expensive for South Africa to buy from other countries.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText: Name any TWO methods of import substitution.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 1 mark per correct method (2 x 1 = 2 marks). Any TWO of:
• Tariffs (ad-valorem tariff, specific tariff)
• Diverting trade / import deposits / quality standards
• Quotas
• Subsidies
• Exchange control
• Physical control / Embargo
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText: How can the government use land restitution to achieve its development and redress objectives?
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks for a correct full-sentence response (1 x 2):
The government can return land or pay cash compensation to those who lost their land because of discriminatory laws in the past, to improve the standard of living for the previously disadvantaged people.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText:
(Refer to the extract 'SOUTH AFRICA'S 2030 ENERGY PLAN' in the question paper.) Identify the energy source that relates to the burning of fossil fuels.

Extract: As part of the 2030 plan, the Department of Mineral Resources and Energy effectively unlocked R56 billion that will be invested in renewable energy projects across the country. Municipalities are required to select suitable off-grid energy sources and to provide access to poor households. [Adapted from Department of Mineral Resources and Energy Statement, 2021]
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: Coal (1 mark)
Coal is a fossil fuel that is burned to generate energy/electricity.

subQuestions.questionText: Give the index that is used to measure society's level of development.
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: Human Development Index / HDI (1 mark)
The Human Development Index measures a society's level of development using life expectancy, education and per capita income.

subQuestions.questionText: Briefly describe the term economic indicator.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks for a correct description:
An economic indicator is statistical data used to measure the performance of the economy / statistical information used by government to determine future economic policy and to make predictions about the future performance of the economy.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText: Explain the negative impact of rural-urban migration on the supply of services in urban areas.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks for a correct explanation:
• Population increases in urban areas will put more pressure on the supply of services such as water and sanitation.
• Provision of housing will be unable to meet demand, resulting in informal settlements without proper infrastructure.
• Electricity demands in urban areas will put pressure on the power grid, leading to more load shedding.
• Constraints on local government regarding local budget and planning.
• Unlawful occupation of land that was set aside for agricultural production.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText: How will renewable sources of energy affect poor households in rural areas positively?
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks per correct explanation (2 x 2 = 4 marks):
• The cost of living for the households will decrease as they pay less for electricity/energy, resulting in an improved standard of living.
• Households will have more disposable income to spend on other basic goods and services.
• Electricity becomes more accessible to vulnerable communities.
• Clean energy sources will impact positively on the health of communities.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText:
(Refer to the infographic 'Special Economic Zones' in the question paper.) Identify the financial incentive that allows for the importing of intermediate goods without paying any tariffs.

Infographic: Special Economic Zones — The SEZ programme attracted 234 investors, creating 15 000 direct jobs. … offers Duty-free incentives, Foreign Investment Grant and Skills Support Programme. Tax incentives. [Adapted from Google, SEZ latest development, March 2021]
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: Duty-free (incentive) (1 mark)
A duty-free incentive allows businesses in a special economic zone to import intermediate goods without paying any import tariffs.

subQuestions.questionText: Name any ONE special economic zone in South Africa.
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: any ONE (1 mark). Acceptable answers include:
• Coega SEZ (Eastern Cape)
• Richards Bay SEZ (KZN)
• East London SEZ (Eastern Cape)
• Saldanha Bay SEZ (Western Cape)
• Dube Tradeport SEZ (KZN)
• Maluti-a-Phofung SEZ (Free State)
• OR Tambo IDZ (Gauteng)
• Musina/Makhado SEZ (Limpopo)
• Atlantis SEZ (Western Cape)
• Nkomazi SEZ (Mpumalanga)
• Tshwane Automotive SEZ

subQuestions.questionText: Briefly describe the term corridors.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks for a correct description:
A corridor is a track of land that forms a passageway allowing access from one area to another and is developed as part of regional development.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText: How is the government using corporate tax to attract investments into special economic zones?
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks for a correct explanation:
• The government reduced corporate tax from 27% to 15% for businesses that are established in SEZs.
• The tax relief makes it possible for new businesses to survive the first few years in production by reducing operational cost for them.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText: Explain the importance of public-private partnerships in spatial development initiatives.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks per correct explanation (2 x 2 = 4 marks):
• It allows private sector businesses to take advantage of the economic potential of underdeveloped areas.
• The private business may provide investment capital, while government provides infrastructure such as roads, water and electricity.
• More factors of production will be employed as more investments are attracted.
• Businesses benefit from profits and government benefits from taxes, levies and decreased unemployment.
• Allows moving towards international competitiveness, regional cooperation and a more diverse ownership base.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText: Outline the aims of regional development.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks per correct aim (4 x 2 = 8 marks). Maximum 4 marks for mere listing of facts/examples:
• Reduce unequal development of economic activities within a country.
• Stimulate development in poorer areas.
• Prevent new imbalances from emerging / enhance the competitiveness of all provinces.
• Implement and coordinate the implementation of national and regional industrial policies.
• Stimulate the growth of SMMEs in the economy.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText: Analyse the environmental effects of economic activities of countries in the north.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award up to 8 marks (2 marks per fully developed point). Maximum 2 marks for mere listing of facts/examples:
• Mass production and consumption in the north damage the ozone layer, caused by pollution and toxic substances.
• Northern countries are guilty of being big burners of oil and coal where CO2 damages the environment and creates climate change experienced worldwide.
• Greenhouse gases produced by large industries affect lives in the south more negatively due to their way of living.
• Climate change has necessitated international agreements like the Kyoto Protocol, to reduce greenhouse gases.
• Climate change results in less agricultural output due to poor soil conditions, inadequate and unreliable rainfall.
• The south is badly affected by degradation of land and contamination of water and vegetation which causes malnutrition and hunger.
• Trade expansion can have an obvious direct impact on the environment due to higher pollution or degrading natural resources.
• Open markets can improve access to new technologies that make local production processes more efficient by diminishing the use of inputs such as energy, water, and other environmentally harmful substances.
• As a country becomes more integrated within the world economy, its export sector becomes more exposed to environmental requirements imposed by the leading importers.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText: Name any TWO international benchmark criteria for regional development.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 1 mark per correct criterion (2 x 1 = 2 marks). Any TWO of:
• Free-market operation
• Competitiveness
• Sustainability
• Good governance
• Provision of resources
• Investment in social infrastructure
• Integration
• Partnerships
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText: Why are liabilities added when calculating net direct investments in the financial account of the balance of payments?
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks for a correct full-sentence response (1 x 2):
Liabilities represent a capital inflow or money flow from the foreign sector into South Africa.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText:
(Refer to the extract 'WHY DO COUNTRIES TRADE?' in the question paper.) Identify the supply reason for international trade addressed in the extract above.

Extract: Today, international trade is at the heart of the global economy and is responsible for much of the development and prosperity of the modern industrialised world. Countries trade with each other when they do not have the resources, or capacity, to satisfy their own needs and wants. By exploiting their domestic scarce natural resources, countries can produce a surplus and trade this for the resources they need. Faced by large global markets, firms may be encouraged to adopt mass production and apply new technology. [Adapted from www.internationalecon.com]
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: Natural resources / Technology (1 mark)
The extract refers to countries exploiting their domestic scarce natural resources (and applying new technology) as supply-side reasons for international trade.

subQuestions.questionText: Name the product explicitly recorded in the current account, due to its historic importance.
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: Gold (1 mark)
Gold is recorded explicitly (as a separate item) in the current account of the balance of payments because of its historic importance to South Africa.

subQuestions.questionText: Briefly describe the term mass production.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks for a correct description:
Mass production is the production of goods in large quantities which may reduce the average cost of production.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText: Explain the reason for South African consumers importing products that are available on domestic markets.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks for a correct explanation:
• Imported products may be of better quality than local products.
• Imported products may be available at lower prices.
• Some local consumers enjoy shopping exclusively because of brand loyalty, an increase in income and different tastes.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText: How could natural disasters, such as a drought, influence the South African trade balance?
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks per correct explanation (2 x 2 = 4 marks):
• Reduced local agricultural production will result in a decrease in exports.
• Local consumers will be forced to import more food products due to shortages on local markets.
• The trade balance will weaken as exports decrease while imports increase.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText:
(Refer to the extract 'SOUTH AFRICA'S ECONOMY HITS LOW' in the question paper.) Identify ONE component of aggregate demand in the information above.

Extract: South Africa's gross domestic product (GDP) fell by just over 16,4% between the first quarter and second quarter of 2020, resulting in an annualised growth rate of 51%. The demand side of the economy slumped by 52,3% as a result of lower exports and household spending. [Adapted from @StatsSA, February 2021]
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: any ONE (1 mark):
• Exports
• Household spending / consumer spending

subQuestions.questionText: Name the employment indicator that relates to the size of the labour force in the country.
subQuestions.memoText:
Correct answer: Economically active population / EAP (1 mark)
The economically active population (labour force) reflects the size of the labour force willing and able to work.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText: Briefly describe the term economic growth.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks for a correct description:
Economic growth is an increase in the production of goods and services over time / an increase in real GDP.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText: Explain the impact of an increase in consumer spending on the production of goods and services.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks for a correct explanation:
Demand for goods and services will increase, encouraging businesses to produce more.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText: How can small, medium and microenterprises (SMMEs) contribute to economic growth and development?
subQuestions.memoText:
Award 2 marks per correct explanation (2 x 2 = 4 marks):
• More job opportunities will be created in both the formal and informal sectors, resulting in more sources of income.
• An increase in aggregate demand will lead to higher production levels.
• Competition will increase, resulting in lower prices for goods and services.
• Tax revenue for the government will increase, leading to more social expenditure on the poor.
• Surplus products will be exported, and foreign currency will be earned to pay for imported inputs.
• Government support to create programmes for the training of workers.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText: Briefly discuss exchange rate stability and price stability as macroeconomic objectives of the state.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award up to 8 marks (2 x 4). Maximum 4 marks for mere listing of facts/examples:

Exchange rate stability:
• Depreciation and appreciation of a currency create uncertainty for producers and traders and should therefore be limited.
• The government should manage the economy through monetary and fiscal policies so that the exchange rate remains relatively stable for as long as possible.
• South Africa pursues stable exchange rates to attract foreign capital.

Price stability:
• In a mixed economy, prices fluctuate as demand and supply change.
• Frequent and dramatic changes in prices affect economic growth and employment.
• The government attempts to guard against price instability.
• In South Africa, price stability means an inflation rate of between 3% and 6%.
• Stable prices enable firms and households to predict income and expenditure.
• Investor confidence is boosted by stable prices and attracts foreign direct investment.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText: Analyse the challenges of the South African government in reducing the unemployment rate in the economy.
subQuestions.memoText:
Award up to 8 marks (2 marks per fully developed point). Maximum 2 marks for mere listing of facts/examples:
• Corruption among state-owned enterprises creates negative sentiment among potential investors.
• Lack of skills among the South African youth reduces the employability of many people.
• Lack of information among some of the youth reduces accessibility of employment opportunities.
• The Covid-19 recession resulted in thousands of workers losing their jobs, sharply increasing the unemployment rate.
• Negative sentiment towards the economy resulted in less foreign direct investment.
• Lack of start-up capital among the youth results in many potential entrepreneurial ideas not being invested in.
• Poor infrastructure in some regions of the country reduces industrial activities in such areas.
• Unreliable electricity supply further cripples any prospects of increasing job opportunities in South Africa.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

subQuestions.questionText:
Essay Question (40 marks – 40 minutes):
• Discuss in detail the new economic paradigm in smoothing-out business cycles. (26)
• Evaluate the South African government's initiatives to reduce the economic downturn caused by the Covid-19 pandemic. (10)

Structure of essay:
- Introduction (Max 2 marks)
- Body: Main Part (Max 26 marks) - max 8 marks for headings/examples
- Body: Additional Part (Max 10 marks) - max 2 marks for mere listing
- Conclusion (Max 2 marks)
subQuestions.memoText:
ESSAY MARK ALLOCATION:
• Introduction: Max 2
• Body – Main part: Max 26
• Body – Additional part: Max 10
• Conclusion: Max 2
TOTAL: 40

INTRODUCTION (Max 2):
• The new economic paradigm suggests that it is possible to implement measures to promote economic growth and reduce unemployment without provoking inflation.
• The new economic paradigm is embedded in both demand-side and supply-side policies.
(Accept any other relevant introduction.)

BODY: MAIN PART (Max 26):

Demand-side policies:
• Traditional monetary and fiscal policies focus on aggregate demand.

Monetary policy:
• When the level of economic activity is depressed, the SARB can use expansionary measures to stimulate economic activities.
• An expansionary monetary policy is implemented when the economy is in recession in order to stimulate economic activities.
• Interest rates can be reduced to make borrowing cheaper and encourage spending by households and businesses.
• The increased spending increases the level of economic activity; investment will increase and more factors of production will be employed.
• Higher levels of production, income and expenditure will be achieved.
• If the supply of goods and services does not increase in line with the increase in demand, inflation will increase.

Fiscal policy:
• When the level of economic activity is low, the Minister of Finance can use expansionary fiscal measures to stimulate growth and reduce unemployment.
• An expansionary fiscal policy can be implemented when the economy is in recession in order to stimulate economic activities.
• An increase in government expenditure will increase aggregate demand.
• When there is an increase in injection in the economy, production increases, resulting in a higher employment of factors of production.
• The result will be higher income and higher expenditure.
• Taxes can be reduced, which will lead to an increase in disposable income.
• This will increase consumer spending and investment, stimulating aggregate demand.

Inflation:
• When demand increases, supply will react in the same way.
• If the supply does not react to an increase in demand, prices will increase (a new equilibrium).
• Aggregate demand and supply are in equilibrium where AD = AS at point C, and again where AD1 = AS1 at point E.
• If AD1 increases and AS does not respond, the new equilibrium will be at point F; real production will increase and prices will also increase. Inflation will prevail.
(Graph – AD/AS: Labelling of axis = 1 mark; Labelling of curves = 1 mark; Shifting of AD and AS = 2 marks. Max 4 marks.)

Unemployment:
• Demand-side policies are effective in stimulating economic growth.
• The demand for labour will increase due to economic growth, which leads to reduced unemployment.
• A decrease in unemployment results in an increase in inflation because more people are employed, which causes an increase in demand for labour.
• This relationship between unemployment and inflation is illustrated using the Phillips curve.
• The Phillips curve shows the relationship between unemployment and inflation.
• Supply-side measures can relocate the Phillips curve to shift it to the left, due to improved education, effective training and fewer restrictions on the immigration of skilled workers.
(Phillips-curve graph: Labelling of axes = 1 mark; Labelling of curve = 1 mark; Labelling on axes = 1 mark; Correct shape of PC = 1 mark. Max 4 marks.)

Supply-side policies:
• A demand-side approach does not render a desirable outcome because growth has to be cut due to problems with inflation.
• Aggregate supply needs to be managed as well by focusing on increased flexibility of supply components.
• If the cost of increasing production is completely flexible, a greater output can be supplied at any given price level.
• Government can arrange things in the economy in a way that is cooperative to changes in demand.
• Reduction of costs allows greater output to be supplied at any given price level.

Government measures that can reduce costs:
• Infrastructural services like communication, transport and energy costs.
• Administrative costs like inspections and regulations that add to overall costs.
• Cash incentives such as subsidies lower the production cost.
• Compensation to exporters to encourage increased production aimed at foreign markets.

Measures to improve efficiency of inputs:
• Lower rates of personal income tax are incentives for high productivity and increase aggregate supply.
• Capital consumption by replacing capital goods on a regular basis creates opportunities for businesses to keep up with technological development.
• Human resources development where the quality of labour can be improved through health care, education and training, increasing the efficiency of businesses.
• Free advisory services to promote opportunities to export and establish business activities in foreign countries (weather forecasts, veterinary services and research).

Measures to improve efficiency of markets:
• Deregulation where laws and regulations are removed to make markets free.
• Competition is encouraged to establish new businesses, invite foreign direct investment and remove power imbalances.
• Levelling the economic playing fields because private businesses cannot compete with public enterprises due to legislative protection.
(Accept any other correct relevant response. Maximum 8 marks for mere listing of facts/examples.)

ADDITIONAL PART (Max 10):
• Reduction in the repo rate to keep the cost of borrowing low has stimulated consumer spending and investment.
• Loan guarantees for businesses with low turnover have helped them survive extra costs brought by Covid-19.
• Relaxing regulatory requirements has supported the flow of credit to households and businesses.
• The government introduced temporary payment holidays and other measures to support debtors.
• Tax deferral and postponement of new taxes have encouraged businesses to continue operating, saving several jobs.
• The temporary employment relief scheme has supported workers and reduced retrenchments.
• Expansion of social grants and other social relief increased demand for goods and services, encouraging businesses to produce more.
• Reallocation of funds among government departments resulted in some departments failing to deliver services, e.g. infrastructure development.
• Restrictions on the trading of non-essential products such as alcohol and tobacco resulted in a decline in tax revenue for the government.
• Borrowing of funds to fight the pandemic has increased the public debt.
(Accept any other correct higher-order relevant response.)

CONCLUSION (Max 2):
It is critically important for the government to focus on both demand-side and supply-side measures to ensure stability in the economy.
(Accept any other correct higher-order relevant conclusion.)

subQuestions.questionText:
Essay Question (40 marks – 40 minutes):
• Discuss the arguments in favour of protectionism. (26)
• How can South Africa benefit from trading in global markets? (10)

Structure of essay:
- Introduction (Max 2 marks)
- Body: Main Part (Max 26 marks) - max 8 marks for headings/examples
- Body: Additional Part (Max 10 marks) - max 2 marks for mere listing
- Conclusion (Max 2 marks)
subQuestions.memoText:
ESSAY MARK ALLOCATION:
• Introduction: Max 2
• Body – Main part: Max 26
• Body – Additional part: Max 10
• Conclusion: Max 2
TOTAL: 40

INTRODUCTION (Max 2):
Protectionism is a trade policy whereby the state implements measures to protect local industries against unfair competition from abroad.
(Accept any other correct relevant response.)

BODY: MAIN PART (Max 26):

Industrial development:
• Some developing countries are suitable for establishing certain kinds of industries.
• Free trade makes it impossible to compete with well-established older countries, due to the first few years of existence of an industry being the most difficult.
• Older industries use unfair methods of price-cutting and dumping – therefore young industries need protection until properly established.
• Protection will prevent competition, because it is difficult to do away with once applied.

Infant industries:
• It is difficult for a young industry to survive, due to their average costs being higher than those of well-established foreign competitors.
• If they are given protection in their early years, they may grow and take advantage of economies of scale / lower their average costs / become competitive.

Stable wage levels and high standard of living:
• A country with high wages has a view that the standard of living will be undermined if cheaper goods are imported from countries with low wages.
• In reality, high wages are paid to workers with high productivity.

Increased employment:
• Local industries that cannot find profitable markets may stop production and cause unemployment.
• Protection will result in less unemployment.

Economic self-sufficiency and strategic key industries:
• War causes cut-offs, or friction between countries, depression and shifts in demand, all factors that make it vital to be self-supporting.
• Protection is granted especially to key industries to ensure survival.

Maintaining domestic employment, to reduce unemployment and provide more job opportunities:
• Countries with high levels of unemployment are pressured to stimulate employment creation.
• Protectionist policies are used to stimulate industrialisation.
• Domestic employment is encouraged through imposing import restrictions.
• Domestic employment creation at the expense of other countries is known as 'Beggar thy neighbour' policies.

Prevent dumping:
• Countries sell goods in a foreign country at lower prices than the cost of production in the home country.
• Dumping is used to capture new markets and forces financially weaker industries out of competition.
• Foreign enterprises may engage in dumping because government subsidies permit them to sell goods at very low prices or below cost, or because they are seeking to raise profits through price discrimination.
• The initial reason for exporting products at a low price may be to dispose of accumulated stocks of goods.
• In the short term, consumers in the importing country will benefit.
• However, their long-term objective may be to drive out domestic producers and gain a strong market position.
• In this case consumers are likely to lose out as a result of the reduction in choice and the higher prices that the exporters will be able to charge.
• Protectionism prevents foreign industries from dumping their surpluses and out-of-season goods at low prices, which may be harmful to home industries.

Stabilising exchange rates and balance of payments:
• Traders buy on the cheapest markets and sell on the most expensive ones.
• Countries export primary products and import manufactured goods, causing a disrupted balance of payments and exchange rates.
• Prices of imports increase through tariffs and quotas.
• A stable exchange rate and BoP increases government revenue / prevents harmful goods from entering the country / develops greater technical skills.

Protection of natural resources:
• Free trade will exhaust resources because the world shares them.
• Protection ensures that industries survive.

Ensures greater economic stability:
• Over-specialisation is a result of free trade and is harmful in times of war and friction (more guns than food).
• Protection prevents over-specialisation, thereby creating a more differentiated economy and greater stability.
• It also promotes secondary industries and the welfare of people dependent on protected industries.
• If imports are greater than exports, a country may introduce import controls such as customs duty and quotas to eliminate the deficit on the balance of payments.
• Developing countries rely on the export of primary products. Selling processed goods is more beneficial as more foreign exchange can be earned; protection ensures the processing of primary goods until completion.
(Accept any other correct relevant response. Maximum 8 marks for mere listing of facts/examples.)

ADDITIONAL PART (Max 10) – South Africa will benefit from global markets as follows:
• Production of goods and services will increase as local businesses sell their products to larger markets.
• Quality of goods and services will improve as businesses try to match world standards.
• Competition from foreign products will encourage local businesses to be more innovative.
• Efficiency in the production of goods and services will improve, resulting in businesses charging lower prices.
• South African consumers will have more choice of goods and services, as they will have access to foreign products.
• More job opportunities may be created as the production of goods and services increases.
• Inflation may be controlled as local prices will be linked to international prices.
• South Africa will increase its trade relations with other countries, resulting in a larger market share internationally.
• Foreign currency will be earned which will strengthen the domestic currency.
• South Africa will specialise in the production of goods in which it has a comparative advantage.
(Accept any other correct higher-order relevant response.)

CONCLUSION (Max 2):
The policy of restriction of international trade (protectionism), with the aim of preventing unemployment or capital losses in industries threatened by imports, might not affect the internal distribution of income sufficiently or improve the country's terms of trade, because it is not based on international monopoly power and expert knowledge.
(Accept any other correct higher-order relevant conclusion.)
